name: Orthodontic retainer
lead: An orthodontic retainer is a custom appliance, either removable (wire-and-acrylic Hawley or clear vacuum-formed plastic) or fixed (a wire bonded behind the front teeth), worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their new positions [1][2]. Its purpose is to limit relapse, the tendency of teeth to drift back, which is attributed to periodontal fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure, occlusion and continued growth [2].

Reviews of the orthodontic literature emphasise that retention should be planned in advance, may vary in duration, and depends on patient compliance [1]. In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are discussed mainly in relation to whether wearing or stopping them affects jaw, palate or facial growth, a claim for which the sources reviewed contain no supporting studies.
infobox: Set by the orthodontist; fixed or indefinite [2]

paras: Removable options include the Hawley retainer (metal wire with acrylic base, the oldest type), the clear vacuum-formed retainer, and variants of these [1][2]. Fixed retainers are wires bonded to the tongue side of the front teeth, requiring less patient cooperation but harder to clean [2]. Newer removable cases linked to a phone app track and remind wear [2].

Wikipedia notes that relapse is more likely when removable retainers are not worn consistently, that one cited review found Hawley retainers ineffective at preventing incisor crowding relapse, that vacuum-formed retainers appear better for lower incisors, and that fixed retainers gave the best retention [2]. A randomised trial examined whether audiovisual instructions and weekly reminders improved retainer wear compliance [4]. Cost and satisfaction comparisons of Hawley and vacuum-formed retainers have also been published [5].

Poor cleaning can lead to decay and gum inflammation, particularly with fixed retainers [2]. A systematic review describes "wire syndrome", unintended tooth movement that can occur even with an intact bonded retainer wire, as an undesirable event distinct from relapse [3].

Forum threads on looksmax.org ask whether long-term retainer wear removes the chance of natural forward growth [6], whether a bonded retainer harms facial structure [7], and whether retainers can be used to expand the palate or combined with mewing [8][9]. The orthodontic sources reviewed describe retainers as maintaining tooth position, not as growth-modifying appliances [1][2].

Randomised trials compare retainer types for compliance, cost and clinical performance [4][5][10]. A systematic review of bonded retainers documents wire syndrome as a complication [3]. No studies found on retainers affecting facial growth or appearance beyond tooth alignment.

lore.intro: Retainers are discussed on looksmax.org mostly as something that might help or hinder jaw and palate development.

claims.claim: Long-term retainer wear "kills" natural forward growth
claims.believers: A poster who had worn a retainer for about five years asked whether removing it could allow forward growth to resume [6].
claims.experts: Orthodontic reviews describe retainers as holding tooth position after treatment [1][2]; no studies in the sources reviewed test an effect on forward facial growth.

claims.claim: A retainer can expand the palate or be combined with mewing
claims.believers: Threads propose using a retainer to widen the palate or a custom "mewing retainer" [8][9].
claims.experts: Retainers are described as passive appliances for retention [1]; palate widening is done with dedicated expanders.

card.summary: The post-braces appliance that keeps teeth where they were moved; proven for retention, untested for jaw growth.
card.note: Bonded wires can cause unintended tooth movement; no evidence it changes facial growth.

quick.overview:
A retainer holds teeth in place after braces or aligners, either as a removable plastic or wire device or a wire bonded behind the teeth.

Its evidence is for keeping teeth aligned. Forum claims that retainers help or block jaw and palate growth have not been studied.
quick.mechanism: Passive pressure or a bonded wire keeps teeth from drifting back while surrounding fibres adapt.
quick.risks: Poor hygiene can cause decay or gum inflammation; bonded retainers can cause unwanted tooth movement (wire syndrome); removable ones can break or warp.
